text: Hi, how's it going? I'm a big coffee lover, so I guess I'll start there. I can't really start my day without a cup of coffee, and this morning was no different. I had one before I came to take this test, and I'm already looking forward to another one once it's over. I work in IT, and my days are pretty busy. I live in an apartment, and I'm pretty much a homebody. In my free time, I like listening to music, playing computer games, and reading. So, yeah, that's me in a nutshell: coffee, music, and my computer. I'm happy to be here, and I hope I do well today!

Well, Korea has four distinct seasons, and each one has its own personality. Spring is my favorite. It's warm and sunny, and the cherry blossoms are everywhere, but the yellow dust can be a pain. Summer is hot and sticky, and then the rainy season hits and it pours for weeks. I can't live without air conditioning in July! Fall is the best time of the year. The sky is clear, the air is crisp, and the leaves turn red and gold. Winter is cold and dry, and it can drop below freezing, though where I live it's a bit milder than in Seoul. So, to sum up, I'd say you get a little bit of everything, and that's what makes living here fun.

Let me think, it's a beautiful fall day today. The sky is totally clear, and the sun is out, but there's a chilly breeze. When I left home this morning, I could see my breath! I almost forgot my jacket, but my mom texted me, "It's cold out there!" So I grabbed it at the last minute. By noon, it warmed up a bit, and it felt just right. Honestly, this is my kind of weather: not too hot, not too cold. It's perfect for a hot cup of coffee, which I had on the way here, of course.

Looking back, the weather has changed a lot. When I was a kid, winters were really cold and snowy. I remember waking up to a yard full of snow. My friends and I would run outside and build a huge snowman. My mom would yell, "Come in before you freeze!" but we never listened. The pond near our house froze solid, so we even slid on the ice. These days, it's totally different. Winters are warmer, and it hardly snows in my city anymore. On the other hand, summers have gotten brutal, with heat waves and crazy rain. I think it's because of global warming. I honestly miss those snowy winters.

Sure, I live in an apartment in a small city by the sea. When you walk in, you see a small entrance with a shoe rack, and the living room is right ahead. It's not huge, but it feels warm and homey. We have two bedrooms: one for sleeping and one I use as a study. We also have a kitchen with a dining table, a bathroom, and a little balcony where I grow a few plants. The windows face a small garden, so it's nice and quiet. It's not fancy, but it's home sweet home. After a long day at work, I can't wait to walk through that door.

On weekdays, my routine is pretty boring. I get home around seven, have dinner and relax for a bit. Then I jump on the computer to check work emails or play a game to clear my head. Before bed, I read a few pages of a book. On weekends, it's a different story. The first thing I do is make a cup of hand-drip coffee. I grind the beans myself, and the whole house smells amazing. Then I do some cleaning and a bit of grocery shopping. In the afternoon, I'm usually glued to my computer, and in the evening, I eat pizza and watch a movie. That's my idea of a perfect weekend.

There's one problem I'll never forget. It happened last summer on a Sunday morning. I was sipping coffee on the couch when my doorbell rang like crazy. It was my downstairs neighbor, and he said, "Water is dripping from my ceiling!" I ran to the laundry room, and it was a total mess. The washing machine hose had come loose, and water was flooding the floor. I turned off the water valve and grabbed every towel in the house. I mopped for an hour. Then I went downstairs to apologize. His ceiling had a big wet stain, and I felt awful. I called a repairman and paid for the damage. To make a long story short, it cost me a small fortune, but my neighbor was really nice about it. Now I check that hose every month!

If I had to pick one, I'd say Japan. It's super popular with Koreans, and there are a few reasons why. First of all, it's really close. From Busan, it takes about an hour by plane, so you can go for a weekend. Second, it's easy on the wallet compared to Europe. And third, the food is amazing: ramen, sushi, and all kinds of street food. People also love the shopping, especially in Osaka and Fukuoka. I'd say the best part is that it feels safe and clean. You don't have to worry about much, even if you don't speak Japanese. So, it's no wonder that so many people head there every holiday.

When I was about ten, my family took a trip to China. We went to Qingdao by ferry for my cousin's wedding. It was my first time on a big ship, and I was so excited that I couldn't sleep. I ran around the deck like a crazy kid. When we got there, everything was so different. The streets were huge, the signs were in Chinese, and the food smelled totally new. I remember eating huge steamed buns and trying beer for the first time, just a sip, and I made a face! My cousins cracked up. My impression was that China was so big and full of energy. Even now, whenever I smell steamed buns, I think of that trip.

Oh, I have one for sure. A friend and I went to Bangkok a few years ago. After a long flight, we waited at the baggage claim, and waited, and waited. Our suitcases never showed up! I was like, "You've got to be kidding me!" The airline said they'd lost our bags, and they didn't know when they'd find them. We were stuck with only what we were wearing. So we ended up shopping at a night market for T-shirts and shorts. I looked like a tourist in a bright elephant shirt! We laughed about it the whole time. On the third day, the airline delivered the bags to our hotel at midnight. It was a total pain, but it turned out to be a fun story. Now I always pack a spare shirt in my carry-on.

Hello, I have a job interview with your company next week, and I'd like to ask a few questions if that's okay. First, could you tell me a little bit about what the company does?. I see. And how many employees do you have?. Great. What's the company culture like? Is it more casual or more formal?. Got it. Also, what should I wear to the interview?. One last thing: how long will the interview take, and who will be interviewing me?. That's very helpful. Thank you so much for your time, and I look forward to meeting you!

Hello, I'm so sorry to bother you, but I have some bad news. I can't make it to my interview tomorrow. I suddenly came down with a high fever last night, and I need to see a doctor. I feel terrible, because I was really looking forward to this interview. But I don't want to lose this opportunity, so I have a few ideas. First, could we reschedule it for later this week? I'm free any time after Thursday. Or if that's hard, could we do a video interview while I'm at home? And if neither works, I could do a phone interview during my lunch break. Which option would work best for you? Again, I really apologize for the trouble. Thank you so much for understanding.

Yes, it happened about two years ago. I had an important meeting with a vendor in Seoul, and I'd been preparing for weeks. The night before, a big typhoon hit my city. The wind was crazy, and the news said the main bridge out of town might close. Sure enough, the next morning, it was shut down. I was stuck in town, and there was no way I could get to Seoul. I felt so stressed. So I called the vendor right away and explained the situation. To my relief, he was very understanding. I suggested a video call instead, and he said, "Sure, let's do it." I set up my laptop at home, with the wind howling outside. It was a bit awkward, but the meeting went well. In the end, the deal went through! Since then, I always have a plan B for bad weather.

I'd say they're pretty different. In small towns like mine, everybody knows everybody. So when there's a wedding or a 60th birthday party, the whole neighborhood shows up. People gather at a big hall or even the village square, and the neighbors cook and bring food. It's loud, warm, and a little bit chaotic. Also, older people often lead the party, and there's a lot of singing and dancing. In big cities like Seoul, it's more low-key. People usually invite just close friends and family. They book a nice restaurant or rent a party room, and everything is planned and quick. People are also busy, so they often skip the big party. Personally, I like the small-town way better. It feels more like a real celebration.

Honestly, planning a get-together is harder than it looks. The biggest problem is finding a time that works for everyone. Last year, I tried to organize a reunion with my old college friends. There were ten of us, and everyone had a different schedule. Some had kids, some had business trips, and some lived far away. The group chat blew up with messages, and nobody could agree on anything. Then there's the problem of picking a place, since everyone likes different food. To solve it, I made a simple online poll with three dates. People voted, and we picked the date with the most votes. I also picked a restaurant in the middle of town, so it was easy for everybody. In the end, nine out of ten showed up. I learned that you can't please everyone, but a clear poll helps a lot.
